newsitem.title: JAPAN: US envoy urges Americans to be more aware of Japan.
newsitem.headline: US envoy urges Americans to be more aware of Japan.

text.p: U.S. ambassador to Japan Walter Mondale, in one of his last appearances before returning to private life, on Tuesday urged Americans to be more aware of just how important Japan is to their own future.

"I would say the most important thing Americans need to know, more than I'm afraid is the case, is the importance of Japan to our future -- because everything flows from that," Mondale told a news conference.
"There is some understanding, but sometimes I wonder how deep that is," Mondale said.

"What's been happening here over the last 40 years in terms of economic growth and vitality is unprecedented in the history of the world, and I think we need to make certain that our understanding of this region has caught up with these rapid developments."

Mondale, a former U.S. senator and vice president who ends nearly five decades in public service when he retires on December 15, played a key role in efforts to settle bitter trade feuds and rebuild frayed security ties.

The security alliance was frayed by the end of the Cold War era and jolted by resentment of the huge U.S. military presence on Japan's southern island of Okinawa after the 1995 rape of a Japanese schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen there.
Economic ties were also frazzled when a battle over the car trade took the two nations to the brink of a trade war in 1994.
On Tuesday, however, Mondale said U.S.-Japan security ties were firmer and economic relations better.
"Our security relations, I believe, are on more solid ground and our economic relationship has improved. Human connections between us are growing."

On Monday, the United States and Japan agreed to cut the American presence on Okinawa and announced plans for a floating helicopter base off the island. They also agreed to proceed quickly with talks on plans to strengthen military cooperation.
Mondale stressed -- as he has for his entire tenure -- the importance of the U.S.-Japan security alliance to both nations, and to the region.

"The foundation of the U.S.-Japan relationship remains our security alliance. The United States, Japan and this historically unstable region have an enormous stake in a strong alliance between us," he said.

But again staying true to form, Mondale did not mince words when it came to stressing Washington's desire to see Japan slash the red tape that Tokyo's trade partners say dampens imports and domestic business says stifles entrepreneurship.

"Despite the progress we have made in getting American products into the Japanese market, much remains to be done. As business and political leaders in Japan increasingly recognise, this market remains vastly over-regulated," he said.
He also expressed concern that Japan's traditional emphasis on consensus in decision-making would "continue to frustrate well-intentioned efforts to open the Japanese economy".
Still, Mondale was not completely downbeat about prospects for reform.

"There is a sense of urgency to this in the minds of many Japanese," he said. "I think there are a lot of things coming together here that may bring about a more decisive result on demands for deregulation than the past would suggest is the case."
